rows.verified: DSEAR requires employers to control safety risks from fire, explosion and substances corrosive to metals.
Employers must assess risks caused by dangerous substances before work is carried out.
Dangerous substances include flammable liquids and gases, combustible dusts, gases under pressure and substances corrosive to metal.
Risks must be eliminated or reduced as far as reasonably practicable to protect employees, visitors and members of the public.
Where elimination is not possible, controls should minimise quantities and releases, prevent dangerous atmospheres and avoid ignition sources.
DSEAR requires mitigation, emergency plans, warning arrangements and suitable information, instruction and training.
Employers must classify places where explosive atmospheres may occur and control ignition sources in those areas.
Indoor flammable-liquid quantities should be reduced to the minimum justified by the work activity and risk assessment.
Fire and explosion risk depends on substance properties, quantity, containment, ventilation, ignition sources, process conditions, equipment and emergency controls.
HSE DSEAR evidence is substance-, process-, workplace-, control-, person- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level fire probability.
MERS-CoV is a zoonotic respiratory virus that can be transmitted from dromedary camels to humans.
Middle East respiratory syndrome was first identified in Saudi Arabia and Jordan in 2012.
UKHSA suspect-case assessment considers relevant hospital or camel-related exposure during the 14 days before illness onset.
MERS is a high-consequence infectious disease and suspected cases require urgent discussion with infection services and notification to the health protection team.
MERS can present atypically, including without fever, particularly in immunocompromised patients.
Possible cases not requiring hospital admission should receive self-isolation advice while awaiting test results.
Primary diagnosis uses verified nucleic-acid amplification tests, with reference-laboratory confirmation and characterisation for international reporting.
Non-inactivated suspected MERS samples require containment-level-3 handling and Category B transport under UN3373 packing requirements.
MERS risk depends on destination, hospital or camel exposure, timing, symptoms, immune status, infection-control practice and diagnostic evidence.
UKHSA MERS evidence is traveller-, exposure-, patient-, contact-, laboratory- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection probability.
